html:
Rudaki (about 858 to 941) was a poet and musician at the court of the Samanids in Bukhara, often called the father of New Persian poetry. He was born in Panjrud, a village near Samarkand in what is now Tajikistan.

He was the first major poet to write in New Persian, the language that grew out of Middle Persian and took up the Arabic script after the Arab conquest. The Samanids, who ruled Central Asia and eastern Iran, backed Persian as a language of culture alongside Arabic, and Rudaki was their star, above all under Amir Nasr II. He sang his verses to the harp. Later writers credited him with a vast output, but only a small part survives, including pieces of his verse version of Kalila wa Dimna, the Indian animal fables of the Panchatantra.

Legend says he was born blind; others say he was blinded late in life after falling from favour. His plain, clear style opened the way for Ferdowsi, who began the Shahnameh under the same dynasty. Tajikistan honours Rudaki as its national poet. His patrons also built the Samanid Mausoleum in Bukhara.
